# ADR 0001 — Authentication

- **Status:** accepted (2024-01-15)
- **Deciders:** Platform, Security

## Context

Slate has two audiences that don't overlap. Customers are members of the public:
anonymous until they sign up, hitting the booking app from browsers today and a
planned mobile app, at public traffic volumes. Support agents are employees who
already exist in the company's Okta directory and only ever touch the internal ops
console. We do not want to build and operate our own credential store for staff
(passwords, MFA, offboarding), and customers need an auth mechanism that works from
a native mobile client without a server-rendered session.

## Decision

The two apps authenticate differently because they serve different audiences:

- **Booking app**: short-lived **Bearer JWTs** (15-minute access tokens, refresh
  via cookie) on every `/api/*` endpoint. The token subject is the customer id.
- **Ops console**: **Okta SSO** sessions on every `/ops/*` endpoint, gated on the
  `ops-agent` role. No JWT path.

## Alternatives considered

- **One shared scheme (JWTs for both apps).** Rejected: staff are already in Okta;
  minting our own tokens for employees means a parallel identity store and
  reimplementing offboarding/MFA we get for free from SSO.
- **Server-side session cookies for the booking app.** Rejected: a native mobile
  client is on the roadmap, and stateless bearer tokens travel to mobile far more
  cleanly than a cookie session.
- **Putting agents in the customer identity system.** Rejected: it would blur the
  public/internal boundary and give staff customer-shaped identities with no clean
  place to hang the `ops-agent` role.

## Consequences

- **(+)** Clean public/internal separation; staff auth, MFA, and offboarding are
  owned by Okta; the booking app stays stateless and mobile-ready.
- **(+)** The `ops-agent` role maps to an Okta group, so access changes are an HR/IT
  operation, not a code deploy.
- **(−)** Two auth code paths to build, test, and keep secure — no shared
  middleware between the apps.
- **(−)** JWT refresh, rotation, and revocation add complexity; the 15-minute TTL
  keeps the blast radius of a leaked token small but means frequent refreshes.
- **(−)** All ops work has a hard runtime dependency on Okta availability.
